about: Daily needs of an adult man for the deficiency model (R37.12, M83). Each value names its source. AR = average requirement (half the people need less); AI = adequate intake, set where no AR exists. Thiamin and niacin are per megajoule in EFSA and are converted here at 2,600 kcal (10.88 MJ).

reference.body_weight_source: EFSA DRVs summary report 2017, Table 17 (adult men)

protein.source: EFSA 2017: 0.66 g high-quality protein per kg body weight a day x 68.1 kg

vit_c.source: EFSA 2017 Table 8 (AR set for body saturation, not scurvy); floor: 10 mg a day prevents scurvy (Wikipedia, Scurvy)

vit_a_rae.source: EFSA 2017 Table 8 (ug RE; 1 ug RE = 1 ug retinol = 6 ug beta-carotene). USDA RAE counts beta-carotene at 12:1, so plant foods are slightly undercounted against EFSA

thiamin.source: EFSA 2017 Table 8: 0.072 mg per MJ x 10.88 MJ

niacin.source: EFSA 2017 Table 8: 1.3 mg niacin equivalents per MJ x 10.88 MJ. USDA niacin is preformed niacin only (tryptophan not counted), so protein-rich foods are undercounted

b12.source: EFSA 2017 Table 9 (cobalamin AI; no AR set)

iron.source: EFSA 2017 Table 4, set with 16 % absorption. FAO/WHO 2004 (ch. 13): about 15 % in a good Western diet, 18 % with very high meat intake, 12 % or 10 % with less meat and fish, low in vegetarian diets; high absorption goes with meat, vitamin C with meals, little phytate-rich cereal, and no coffee or tea within two hours of meals

zinc.source: EFSA 2017 Table 4: AR by daily phytate intake

sodium.source: Dietary Reference Intakes for Japanese (2025), minerals chapter 3-1-2: unavoidable losses under 500 mg a day, about 600 mg (1.5 g salt) with 10 % variation, for sedentary adults without sweating; WHO guidance puts the minimum at 200-500 mg a day; heavy sweating in heat or labour loses a corresponding amount of sodium
